title: What is machine learning?
intro: What machine learning actually is, how it differs from ordinary programming, when you should and should not use it — and why generalising is the core concept.

sections.title: From writing rules to learning rules

blocks.html: In traditional programming you write the rules yourself: a program is a list of instructions that turns input into output. That works excellently as long as you can write the rules down — computing taxes, sorting a list, validating a form. But for some problems that is impossible: how do you encode in rules what a cat in a photo is? Which combination of words, senders and links makes an email suspicious?

Machine learning flips this around. Instead of writing rules, you give the computer examples — data with the answers attached — and let the computer derive the rules itself. The formal definition: a program learns from experience E with respect to task T and performance measure P, if its performance on T, as measured by P, improves with E.

Example: the spam filter. Task T: classify emails as spam or not spam. Experience E: thousands of examples of emails that people have already labelled. Performance measure P: the fraction of emails classified correctly. If you can name these three for a problem, you have a well-defined ML problem on paper.

Machine learning shines when the pattern is complex (faces, speech, behaviour), when there is lots of data to learn from, and when the environment changes (fraudsters adapt their tactics, so a model that keeps learning stays relevant). Recommendation systems, voice assistants and fraud detection are therefore classic ML applications.

But ML is a tool, not a goal. If the rule is simple and deterministic (salary under a collective agreement), ordinary code is better: faster, cheaper and fully explainable. If every decision must be legally justifiable (admission to a study programme), a black-box model is risky. And with little data a model rarely learns anything reliable.

blocks.html: An ML model can make mistakes and can inherit biases from its data. Always evaluate on unseen data (see the topic Data, features & labels) and keep a human in the loop for risky decisions.

The goal of a model is not to reproduce the training examples perfectly — any memory can do that. The goal is to generalise: make good predictions for data it has never seen. Think of a student practising with old exams: they should not memorise the answers to those old exams, but recognise the underlying patterns so the real exam goes well too.

In scikit-learn, training is called fit — you “fit” the model to the data. A model that scores perfectly on training data but poorly on new data has learned nothing: it memorises instead of understanding. That is called overfitting, and it is the classic pitfall of every ML beginner (and expert). Chapter 1 shows how to detect it with separate train and test data.

Remember this sentence: a model that only performs well on data it has already seen has learned nothing. Almost everything in the workflow — splitting, evaluating, regularising — exists to combat this problem.
